title: Ambapali's garden
hookLine: the courtesan of Vesali refuses a fortune for the Buddha's meal, gives her mango grove to the order, and later becomes a nun

cards: Chariots on the road outside Vesali, going fast. In one of them rides Ambapali, the courtesan of Vesali.
She has just heard the Buddha is staying in her own mango grove, so she drove out, sat with him, and asked him to eat at her house tomorrow. He accepted, by staying silent.
Now, heading home, she meets the chariots of the Licchavi princes, the ruling families of the town, and drives straight at them, axle to axle, wheel to wheel. What's going on, Ambapali?
The Buddha is coming to her house tomorrow, she says. And the princes want that meal for themselves.

teach.b: First, the offer. In the Great Discourse on the Buddha's final journey, the princes ask her to give up the meal, and offer her a great sum of money. She refuses.
Even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, she says, I wouldn't give up this meal. The princes snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman! Second, the Buddha.
The princes ride on to the grove and invite him themselves. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation.
Hers came first, so it stands, even against the princes'. Third, the gift. The next day she serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands.
When the meal is done, she sits to one side and gives the mango grove to the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head. He accepts it. Fourth, later.
Tradition says Ambapali herself went forth as a nun.
Her verses in the Therigatha look back at her own beauty, part by part, her hair, her eyes, her voice, her hands, and how age changed each one.
Verse after verse ends with the same refrain: the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise. A woman who gave away a lovely grove later let go of her own loveliness too, and wrote it down plainly.

how: Ambapali's meal and gift of her grove are read in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, and her verses on aging in the Therigatha.

o: a field of rice the princes planted
a palace garden kept for a king's horses
a mango grove a courtesan gave the monks

p: offered a fortune for the meal
given to the community of monks

s: Ambapali sold the meal to the princes for a fortune
she said she wouldn't give it up even for Vesali and all its lands.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a courtesan invited you first. now the princes who rule the town invite you too. what do you do?
o: accept the princes; they're the rulers.
accept both, and split the day.
games.why: he tells the princes he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. they snap their fingers: beaten by the mango woman.

practice: Think of something you own that's actually beautiful, not just something you're finished with: a book you love, a plant, something you made yourself. Ambapali didn't give leftovers; she gave her grove.
Imagine handing your beautiful thing to someone who would treasure it, and notice what that feels like, without deciding anything.

wordCard.voice: Ambapali's garden. The mango grove the courtesan of Vesali gave to the order, after refusing a fortune for the Buddha's meal. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali amba means mango; tradition says she was found as a baby at the foot of a mango tree.

carryVoice: Your line: the mango grove. First her grove, and later her beauty: she let both go. Until tomorrow.
